entities.name: Pirate Party
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Pirate Party (Piratpartiet), founded January 1, 2006, in Sweden by Rick Falkvinge, is the world's first and globally most influential digital rights political party — established in direct response to the Swedish Antipiracy Bureau's January 2006 police raid on The Pirate Bay servers, growing from Swedish municipal politics to the European Parliament (2 MEPs in 2009, 3 in 2014), inspiring pirate parties in 60+ countries, and fundamentally inserting digital rights, internet freedom, privacy, transparency, and copyright reform into mainstream European political discourse.

Falkvinge launched the party three days after the Pirate Bay raid, gathering 1,000 supporters in 24 hours. The 2009 European Parliament elections — boosted by the Pirate Bay trial (Gottfrid Svartholm, Peter Sunde convicted of copyright infringement in April 2009) — gave the party 7.1% of the Swedish EP vote and 2 seats, making it the EU's first digital rights party in the European Parliament. Pirate parties spread globally: Germany's Piratenpartei entered the Berlin state parliament (2011, 8.9%) and won seats in four German state parliaments; Iceland's Pirate Party polled 22% nationally (2016); Czech Pirates entered government.

The Pirate Party's legacy is primarily discursive: parties that did not survive electorally nonetheless forced major parties to address digital rights, privacy (GDPR), copyright reform, and internet freedom. The 2016 WikiLeaks/Assange era gave pirate politics renewed urgency. Czech Pirate Party (Piráti) entered the Czech governing coalition (2021). The movement pioneered liquid democracy (delegative voting), open source party governance, and unconditional basic income as policy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Pirate Party — emerging from a file-sharing piracy controversy and spreading to 60 countries — proved that a political party founded on digital rights could force GDPR-level privacy legislation and copyright reform by inserting digital issues into mainstream discourse, even when the party itself lost most elections.
